reconcile.connective: Gill treats Luke and John as one scene: dread at Christ's sudden appearance turns to gladness once he shows his wounds.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, lists the two reactions to the same appearance as mutually exclusive, since no one can be terrified and glad at once.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Were the disciples frightened or gladdened when they saw Jesus?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/frightened.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Were the disciples frightened or gladdened when they saw Jesus?"

excerpts.excerpt_text: These he showed, partly to convince them that he was not a spirit, or an apparition, which at first sight they took him to be, from his sudden appearance among them, the doors being locked and barred … then were the disciples glad when they saw the Lord; for by these marks in his hands and feet, and side, they were fully convinced, and entirely satisfied, that it was he; and that he was risen from the dead; and who now appeared to them, than which a more delightful sight could not be enjoyed by them; whereby was fulfilled, what he had foretold and promised, Joh 16:22.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill explicitly frames the wound-showing as proof that dispels the 'spirit'/apparition fear reported in the parallel Luke account, then reports the resulting gladness — bridging Luke's fright and John's joy as sequential stages of one encounter.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714), on John 20:19-23
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats Luke 24:36ff. and John 20:19 as the same appearance, tracing the disciples from the terror of Luke 24:37 to the gladness of John 20:20 once Christ's wounds convinced them. (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies does not appear to treat this specific fear/gladness pairing directly; per spec a row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage is used instead.)
